summary: Extends the SDP grouping framework so several media streams can be tied to a single resource reservation flow. It defines the syntax and a new grouping semantics value called Single Reservation Flow. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a video and its sound should share one reserved lane on the road instead of two. This memo adds a way to say so in the description of a call.

questions: sdp group media streams into one reservation
how to map media streams to one reservation flow
what is the sdp group attribute
how does sdp work with rsvp
subtitle: A way to say in an SDP session description that several media streams should share one resource reservation flow.

tldr.problem: A multimedia session has several media streams, and applications differ on whether they want them in one resource reservation flow or in separate ones. SDP had no way to express that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a new semantics token, Single Reservation Flow (SRF), to the SDP grouping framework. Media lines grouped with SRF should be mapped to the same reservation flow.
tldr.outcome: A session description can now say which streams share a reservation flow, which matters when the remote party takes part in the reservation. The RFC also registers the SRF token with IANA.

today: RFC 3524 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the SRF grouping semantics.

sections.title: Why Streams Need Mapping
sections.content:
Resource reservation protocols give network resources to particular flows of IP packets. A router applies a filter to each packet to find the flow it belongs to, and gives the packet the Quality of Service (QoS) of that flow. Routers typically filter on source and destination IP addresses and port numbers.

A multimedia session usually has several media streams, such as an audio stream and a video stream, and each must be mapped to a reservation flow. Two possible mappings are all streams in one flow, or every stream in its own flow. Some applications need the first, some the second, and some need a mixture: for example, two of three streams in one flow and the third in a second flow.

RFC 3524 defines the SDP syntax to express this mapping, using the SDP grouping framework and a new semantics value called Single Reservation Flow (SRF).
sections.plainLanguage: A call can carry sound and pictures. Sometimes they should share one reserved lane, and sometimes each needs its own. This memo gives a way to say which.

sections.title: SRF Semantics
sections.content:
The RFC defines one new semantics value within the SDP grouping framework: SRF. Media lines grouped with SRF semantics SHOULD be mapped into the same resource reservation flow. Media lines that are not in a given SRF group SHOULD NOT be mapped into the reservation flow used for that group.

An SRF group MAY consist of a single media line. By the definition above, that media line then gets a reservation flow of its own, which carries traffic from that line and from no other.
sections.plainLanguage: If things are in the same SRF group they ride in the same lane. Anything not in the group should stay out of that lane, and a group of one just gets a private lane.

sections.title: When the Mechanism Is Needed
sections.content:
Sometimes the mechanism is unnecessary. Some resource reservation protocols let the entity that generates the SDP session description allocate resources in both directions (that is, sendrecv) for the session. In that case the generator can choose any mapping of media flows to reservation flows it likes.

The mechanism is useful when the remote party needs to be involved in the resource reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you can book the lanes both ways yourself, you do not need to ask anyone. The note matters when the other side has to book part of the lanes.

sections.title: An Example with SIP and RSVP
sections.content:
The example uses SIP to carry the SDP session and RSVP to set up reservation flows, though the RFC says other protocols could be used without changing the SDP syntax. A user agent receives a SIP INVITE with an SDP body that contains the line a=group:SRF 1 2, naming the audio stream (mid 1) and the video stream (mid 2).

Because both streams are in an SRF group, the user agent establishes a single RSVP session. An RSVP session is defined by the triple (DestAddress, ProtocolId[, DstPort]). In the example, the session uses destination address 192.0.0.1, protocol UDP and any destination port.

Had the same user agent received the same media streams without the group line, it would be free to map them into two different RSVP sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The invitation says audio and video are in one group, so the receiver books one lane for both. Without that note it could have booked two.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has registered a new semantics token for the SDP grouping framework in the SDP parameters registry, under Semantics for the group SDP attribute. The entry is named Single Reservation flow, its token is SRF and its reference is RFC 3524.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of allowed words now includes SRF, so everyone uses the same word for the same idea.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who adds group lines with SRF semantics to a session description could force a user agent to set up more or fewer resource reservation flows than needed. That could use up extra resources in the end-point or degrade the quality of service for a session.

The RFC therefore says it is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED that integrity protection be applied to SDP session descriptions. For descriptions carried in SIP, S/MIME is the natural choice for end-to-end integrity protection, as described in RFC 3261. Other applications MAY use a different form of integrity protection.
sections.plainLanguage: If a sneaky person changed the note, you might book too many lanes or too few. Sealing the note so nobody can change it stops that.

viz.caption: SDP WITH AN SRF GROUP (FROM RFC 3524)

data.title: SDP body in the INVITE
data.code:
v=0
o=Laura 289083124 289083124 IN IP4 one.example.com
t=0 0
c=IN IP4 192.0.0.1
a=group:SRF 1 2
m=audio 30000 RTP/AVP 0
a=mid:1
m=video 30002 RTP/AVP 31
a=mid:2
